newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH GOVT BACK INDEPENDENT MARKETS WATCHDOG.
newsitem.headline: CZECH GOVT BACK INDEPENDENT MARKETS WATCHDOG.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said that the government would support the eventual creation of an independent body to supervise local financial markets.
Speaking after a meeting on financial market regulation, he also said that all prices of OTC deals registered at the central securities centre (SCP) would be published from February 1.
Until now Klaus has showed little enthusiasm for a plan by Prague Stock Exchange (PSE) Chairman Tomas Jezek to create a body modelled on the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Foreign investors and some local players have also been highly critical of the lack of general transparency on the Czech capital markets, and particularly about the failure of the SCP, where the overwhelming majority of trades are registered, to release detailed price information.
Klaus has long believed market regulation, now conducted by a department in the Finance Ministry, should be minimal.
But he bowed to pressure by calling a meeting on Sunday of economic ministers plus Jezek and central bank Governor Josef Tosovsky to discuss the situation.

"There is a dominant opinion that there is little transparency on the our capital market," he told reporters after the meeting. "We have agreed that all transactions and their prices which are registered at the SCP will be published." He gave no indication of whether the names of buyers and sellers would also be released.
"As a long-term solution we want to create an independent capital supervision (body). That requires legislation and an number of other things," said Klaus.
Jezek wants to create a Czech SEC by 1998 but Klaus gave no indication of when he thought it could be set up.
Klaus said that as a first step the market supervision department of the Finance Ministry would be transformed into a "Securities Bureau" also from February 1, 1997.

It would remain under the ministry but would have more staff and an 11-member advisory commission for the bureau would also be set up including market participants. The bureau would intensify control of investment funds and companies, he said.
Klaus said that 36 people from government, the central bank, the PSE, commercial banks and market participants had attended the meeting at a chateau outside Prague.

Most of the participants had rejected the idea that trading should be conducted on only one organised market, he said. At present investors can trade on the PSE, the OTC RM-System or merely by registering private deals at the SCP.
Different prices on different markets were a reality in the Czech Republic and the meeting had rejected any attempt to unify prices, said Klaus.

Some analysts have said that a lack of transparency and rampant insider trading have frightened away many foreign investors. The Czech market has underperformed many of its rivals elsewhere in central Europe this year.
But Klaus said the Czech market was moving from its first phase, when it was created under the mass voucher privatisation programme of 1992-95, towards becoming a standard market.
Everybody understood that this process would happen gradually, he added.
